span.label: news values - the criteria by which journalists select stories - and whether a taxonomy of them written before social media still describes what is published
span.quote: News values are worth studying because they inform the mediated world that is presented to news audiences, providing a shared shorthand operational understanding of what working journalists are required to produce to deadlines. It is the way news values work in practice that results in them being articulated and conveyed to new journalism trainees and journalism students, and they are also used by public relations professionals and others aiming to obtain maximum news coverage of events (or pseudo-events).

span.label: to what extent does Harcup and O'Neill's 2001 list of news values remain relevant fifteen years on, and what should be added, split or dropped
span.quote: However, in revisiting our 2001 set of news values, we found that some categories were too broadly deﬁned when subjected to empirical testing; some WHAT IS NEWS? 1479 categories need to be unpicked and some new categories seem to warrant inclusion, and these are put forward in the Conclusion.

span.label: an updated 15-value taxonomy of news values, arrived at by coding 711 stories with the old 10-value list and reporting which of its categories broke under the test - including a value, `shareability`, that did not exist in 2001
span.quote: Although there will be exceptions, we have found that potential news stories must generally satisfy one and preferably more of the following requirements to be selected:

span.label: method
span.quote: Our methodology was deceptively simple if time-consuming: we read each of the 711 stories and used our 2001 set of news values as a coding sheet, identifying which if any of the various factors we could identify in each story. Deciding which news values were present in any particular story involved a close reading of the text, consideration of the content and an evaluation of the context (was it following up a story that had originally been published elsewhere, for example?); the fact that both of us have worked as journalists in addition to studying and teaching journalism perhaps helped in this process. To ensure consistency each story was read and coded by both researchers, with disparities in coding discussed before arriving at consensus.

span.label: a discipline whose central term is defined by its practitioners as `I know it when I see it`, and whose scholars have answered with fifty years of successive taxonomies, each disowned by its own authors
span.quote: Asked how they deﬁne news, journalists sometimes reply: “I know it when I see it.” Pressed on why something has been deemed newsworthy, a typical response is: “Because it just is!” (Brighton and Foy 2007, 147). Deﬁnitions relying on such “gut feeling” (Schultz 2007) arguably obscure as much as they reveal about news selection, prompting academics to offer their own explanations, which can involve devising taxonomies of news values. One of the most inﬂuential and frequently cited of these is a paper by Johan Galtung and Mari Ruge (1965), “The Structure of Foreign News”, published more than 50 years ago.

span.label: content analysis of 711 news-page lead stories across 10 UK newspaper titles from a sample month in 2014, double-coded to consensus against the 2001 news-value list, plus the 25 most-shared UK news stories on Facebook and Twitter that year
span.term: content analysis of 711 news-page lead stories across 10 UK newspaper titles from a sample month in 2014, double-coded to consensus against the 2001 news-value list, plus the 25 most-shared UK news stories on Facebook and Twitter that year
span.quote: This resulted in a data-set of 711 stories, each selected by the newspaper as a news page lead. Each story was then analysed in an effort to identify which, if any, of the Harcup and O’Neill (2001) news values could be detected in the new sample; how news values interact with each other; and whether any amendments, additions or deletions to the list of news values might be considered appropriate.

Pressed on why something has been deemed newsworthy, a typical response is: BECAUSE IT JUST IS!` - and the definitions relying on such gut feeling `arguably OBSCURE AS MUCH AS THEY REVEAL`

span.label: and each break is named: entertainment splits into entertainment and drama, sport joins it, `unusualness` moves into surprise, and large corporations move into the power elite
span.quote: Entertainment encompasses both a dark and light side, which might be better conveyed in two distinct categories. Some of the darker but “entertaining” human-interest stories might perhaps be more accurately labelled as drama. News stories about sport could be added to the entertainment mix alongside show business, while the surprise category ought to contain “unusualness” within its deﬁnition. We also noticed that there were many stories involving large corporations and these might be included within the power elite category.

span.label: `magnitude` is widened because the coding met cases it could not hold - `it ought to include EXTREME BEHAVIOURS OR OCCURRENCES (a man dying in extreme temperatures in an oven, for example, or a particularly unpleasant crime)`
span.quote: On investigation it became apparent that the term “magnitude” can mean more than merely involving large numbers; it ought to include extreme behaviours or occurrences (a man dying in extreme temperatures in an oven, for example, or a particularly unpleasant crime).

span.label: **A NEW VALUE IS ADMITTED FOR A PHENOMENON THAT DID NOT EXIST AT THE LAST REVISION** - `shareability`, and the paper says outright that it is `hard to define`, offering a practitioner's phrase as the nearest thing: `stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry`
span.quote: Precisely what qualities give one story more shareability than another are hard to pin down, but Janine Gibson (a former Guardian website editor who in 2015 became editor-in-chief of BuzzFeed UK) has noted that the most shared stories tend to be “stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry” (quoted in Newman 2011, 24).

span.label: **THE CATEGORIES ARE NOT ALTERNATIVES.** `any taxonomy of news values ought not to be thought of as a LIST OF ALTERNATIVES. It is clear that ONE STORY MIGHT TICK SEVERAL BOXES` - one story was coded good news and bad news at once, and the paper shows the story
span.quote: This ﬁnding that a story might simultaneously be good news and bad news illustrates that any taxonomy of news values ought not to be thought of as a list of alternatives. It is clear that one story might tick several boxes, and how certain news values operate in different combinations might usefully be an issue for future research.

span.label: and the coding's own subjectivity is stated rather than controlled away: `Clearly there is subjectivity involved in such a process - JUST AS THERE IS SUBJECTIVITY INVOLVED IN THE JOURNALISTIC PROCESS ITSELF - and we would never claim anything different`
span.quote: Clearly there is subjectivity involved in such a process—just as there is subjectivity involved in the journalistic process itself—and we would never claim anything different. But we nevertheless believe the sample of stories is large enough to allow for some tentative conclusions to be drawn.

span.label: **Both editions of the list disown themselves.** 2001: offered `NOT AS THE LAST WORD on news values, merely as a contribution towards rendering news selection a more transparent and better-understood process`. 2016: `not something to be CHURNED OUT AS IF IT IS THE LAST WORD on the subject`
span.quote: This was offered, not as the last word on news values, merely as a contribution towards “rendering news selection a more transparent and better-understood process”

span.label: and the paper concedes the practitioners' answer survives its own taxonomy: `whenever the question arises of why a particular story is seen as newsworthy, THERE WILL ALWAYS REMAIN AN ELEMENT OF TRUTH TO THE REPLY: 'IT JUST IS!'`
span.quote: Thus, we reiterate that the above news value taxonomy should be seen as a tool for analysis and further research—designed to provoke discussion and, indeed, contestation— not something to be churned out as if it is the last word on the subject. And, whenever the question arises of why a particular story is seen as newsworthy, there will always remain an element of truth to the reply: “It just is!”

span.label: **the criteria are contestable by construction** - governed by `practical considerations, such as the availability of resources and time, and SUBJECTIVE, OFTEN UNCONSCIOUS, INFLUENCES` including the journalist's position in the workplace hierarchy and the audience being produced for
span.quote: It is important to reiterate that the above criteria can be contested since they are also governed by practical considerations, such as the availability of resources and time, and subjective, often unconscious, inﬂuences, such as a mix of the social, educational, ideological and WHAT IS NEWS? 1483 cultural inﬂuences on journalists, as well as the environment in which they work, their position in the workplace hierarchy and the type of audience for whom journalists are producing news.

span.label: and the authors put the selector above the criteria: `WHO IS SELECTING NEWS, FOR WHOM, IN WHAT MEDIUM AND BY WHAT MEANS ... may well be AS IMPORTANT AS whatever news values may or may not be inherent in any potential story`
span.quote: In other words, who is selecting news, for whom, in what medium and by what means (and available resources), may well be as important as whatever news values may or may not be inherent in any potential story.

span.label: the social media half rests on 25 stories from two `top 10` and `top 15` lists, and the authors call it `necessarily tentative` - noting that people sharing a link `may not normally be readers of the news site` and may be sharing it in disagreement
span.quote: This preliminary examination of how news values operate on social media is necessarily tentative, and it is worth pointing out that many of the people sharing links may not normally be “readers” of the news site in question and may only have come across it via a link in the ﬁrst place. Users of social media may even be sharing links while expressing disagreement with—or disapproval of—a particular item. Such is today’s journalism landscape.

span.label: **and examining output cannot reach intention** - `any exploration of news values can only provide A PARTIAL EXPLANATION of what lies behind journalistic news decisions`, with Staab's functional model, which takes journalists' intentions into account, named as the thing this design cannot do
span.quote: As was stressed in the above study, any exploration of news values can only provide a partial explanation of what lies behind journalistic news decisions. Examining news outputs may explain as much about news treatment as news selection (Staab 1990; Harcup and O’Neill 2001) and Staab (1990) argued for a functional model that takes into account the intentions of journalists.

span.label: extends → Harcup and O'Neill's own 2001 list of ten news values, itself an updating of Galtung and Ruge's 1965 taxonomy - tested here against 711 stories and revised to fifteen
span.quote: 1. The power elite: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organisations or institutions. 2. Celebrity: Stories concerning people who are already famous. 3. Entertainment: Stories concerning sex, showbusiness, human interest, animals, an unfolding drama, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, entertaining photographs or witty headlines. 4. Surprise: Stories that have an element of surprise and/or contrast. 5. Bad news: Stories with particularly negative overtones, such as conﬂict or tragedy. 6. Good news: Stories with particularly positive overtones, such as rescues and cures. 7. Magnitude: Stories that are perceived as sufﬁciently signiﬁcant either in the numbers of people involved or in potential impact. 8. Relevance: Stories about issues, groups and nations perceived to be relevant to the audience. 9. Follow-up: Stories about subjects already in the news. 10. Newspaper agenda: Stories that set or ﬁt the news organisation’s own agenda (Harcup and O’Neill 2001, 278–279).

span.quote: In other words, who is selecting news, for whom, in what medium and by what means (and available resources), may well be as important as whatever news values may or may not be inherent in any potential story.

span.label: **BOTH EDITIONS DISOWN THEMSELVES IN THE SAME WORDS** - 2001 `not as the last word on news values`; 2016 `not something to be churned out as if it is the last word on the subject`, and `there will always remain an element of truth to the reply: It just is!`
span.term: **BOTH EDITIONS DISOWN THEMSELVES IN THE SAME WORDS** - 2001 `not as the last word on news values`; 2016 `not something to be churned out as if it is the last word on the subject`, and `there will always remain an element of truth to the reply: It just is!`
span.quote: Thus, we reiterate that the above news value taxonomy should be seen as a tool for analysis and further research—designed to provoke discussion and, indeed, contestation— not something to be churned out as if it is the last word on the subject. And, whenever the question arises of why a particular story is seen as newsworthy, there will always remain an element of truth to the reply: “It just is!”

span.label: shareability - `Stories that are thought likely to generate sharing and comments via Facebook, Twitter and other forms of social media`, with `stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry` offered as the nearest gloss
span.term: shareability - `Stories that are thought likely to generate sharing and comments via Facebook, Twitter and other forms of social media`, with `stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry` offered as the nearest gloss
span.quote: Precisely what qualities give one story more shareability than another are hard to pin down, but Janine Gibson (a former Guardian website editor who in 2015 became editor-in-chief of BuzzFeed UK) has noted that the most shared stories tend to be “stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry” (quoted in Newman 2011, 24).

span.label: exclusivity - `Stories generated by, or available ﬁrst to, the news organisation as a result of interviews, letters, investigations, surveys, polls`
span.term: exclusivity - `Stories generated by, or available ﬁrst to, the news organisation as a result of interviews, letters, investigations, surveys, polls`
span.quote: Finally, there is a strong case to be made for exclusivity to be considered a news value in its own right, given the frequency with which we found newspapers drawing attention to the fact, as in: “a poll by the Times indicates … ” (24 November 2014) or “It follows an investigation by the Independent … ” (29 November 2014).

span.label: magnitude (revised) - not merely large numbers but `extreme behaviours or occurrences`
span.term: magnitude (revised) - not merely large numbers but `extreme behaviours or occurrences`
span.quote: On investigation it became apparent that the term “magnitude” can mean more than merely involving large numbers; it ought to include extreme behaviours or occurrences (a man dying in extreme temperatures in an oven, for example, or a particularly unpleasant crime).

span.label: news values (2001, ten) - power elite, celebrity, entertainment, surprise, bad news, good news, magnitude, relevance, follow-up, newspaper agenda
span.term: news values (2001, ten) - power elite, celebrity, entertainment, surprise, bad news, good news, magnitude, relevance, follow-up, newspaper agenda
span.quote: 1. The power elite: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organisations or institutions. 2. Celebrity: Stories concerning people who are already famous. 3. Entertainment: Stories concerning sex, showbusiness, human interest, animals, an unfolding drama, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, entertaining photographs or witty headlines. 4. Surprise: Stories that have an element of surprise and/or contrast. 5. Bad news: Stories with particularly negative overtones, such as conﬂict or tragedy. 6. Good news: Stories with particularly positive overtones, such as rescues and cures. 7. Magnitude: Stories that are perceived as sufﬁciently signiﬁcant either in the numbers of people involved or in potential impact. 8. Relevance: Stories about issues, groups and nations perceived to be relevant to the audience. 9. Follow-up: Stories about subjects already in the news. 10. Newspaper agenda: Stories that set or ﬁt the news organisation’s own agenda (Harcup and O’Neill 2001, 278–279).

span.label: stories coded
span.quote: This resulted in a data-set of 711 stories, each selected by the newspaper as a news page lead. Each story was then analysed in an effort to identify which, if any, of the Harcup and O’Neill (2001) news values could be detected in the new sample; how news values interact with each other; and whether any amendments, additions or deletions to the list of news values might be considered appropriate.

span.label: news values in the revised list
span.term: news values in the revised list

span.label: social media stories examined
span.quote: This preliminary examination of how news values operate on social media is necessarily tentative, and it is worth pointing out that many of the people sharing links may not normally be “readers” of the news site in question and may only have come across it via a link in the ﬁrst place. Users of social media may even be sharing links while expressing disagreement with—or disapproval of—a particular item. Such is today’s journalism landscape.

span.label: bad news leads at 442 of 711 - but the paper reports IN THE SAME SECTION that `some categories were too broadly defined when subjected to empirical testing`, and then splits `bad news` to move conflict out of it. **The ranking and the revision are measured with the same instrument, and the revision says the instrument was wrong.**
span.term: **a frequency table over a category set the same paper calls unstable**
span.quote: In considering 711 page lead stories across 10 newspaper titles (see Tables 1 and 2), our ﬁndings show that bad news is the big winner; but good news is still signiﬁcant, and some stories fall into both categories.

span.label: which news values are present in a story - the coded variable, decided by close reading of text, content and context by two researchers to consensus
span.term: which news values are present in a story - the coded variable, decided by close reading of text, content and context by two researchers to consensus
span.quote: Our methodology was deceptively simple if time-consuming: we read each of the 711 stories and used our 2001 set of news values as a coding sheet, identifying which if any of the various factors we could identify in each story. Deciding which news values were present in any particular story involved a close reading of the text, consideration of the content and an evaluation of the context (was it following up a story that had originally been published elsewhere, for example?); the fact that both of us have worked as journalists in addition to studying and teaching journalism perhaps helped in this process. To ensure consistency each story was read and coded by both researchers, with disparities in coding discussed before arriving at consensus.

span.label: who is doing the selecting - journalists in print against audiences sharing on social media, the same instrument applied to both
span.term: who is doing the selecting - journalists in print against audiences sharing on social media, the same instrument applied to both
span.quote: Between the newspaper and social media data-sets, there were some similarities as well as differences; bad news is almost as popular a factor online as in print. However, the most popular stories online are rarely concerned with the power elite. There may be little doubt that digital media can help challenge mainstream news agendas, but the most popular stories do not reﬂect this democratic ideal.
